Well-Posed Learning Problem
content:
A learning problem is precisely defined, or \textbf{well-posed}, once three components are clearly identified:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em]
\item \textbf{Task $T$:} the specific job the program is learning to perform.
\item \textbf{Performance measure $P$:} a measurable quantity that tells us how well the program is doing at $T$.
\item \textbf{Experience $E$:} the data or interaction the program learns from.
\end{itemize}

Distinguishing the Four Types at a
content:
\textbf{Distinguishing the Four Types at a Glance:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Ask first: \textbf{does every example have a label?} If yes $\to$ Supervised. If none do $\to$ Unsupervised.
\item Ask: \textbf{are only some examples labeled?} If a small labeled portion is combined with a larger unlabeled portion $\to$ Semi-Supervised.
\item Ask: \textbf{is there an agent taking actions and receiving rewards over time}, rather than a fixed dataset at all? If yes $\to$ Reinforcement Learning.
\item These four categories map directly onto Chapters 2 through 4 of these notes, and set up exactly the kind of learning problem studied in the rest of this chapter: Concept Learning (Section 1.2) is a form of supervised learning.
\end{enumerate}

section: Concept Learning and General-to-Specific Ordering of Hypotheses
title: Concept Learning
content: Concept learning is the task of inferring a boolean-valued target function (a \textbf{concept}, such as "EnjoySport = Yes") from a set of training examples, each described by attribute values and labeled as a positive or negative instance of the concept. The learner searches through a space of candidate \textbf{hypotheses} to find one that best explains the training examples.

section: Concept Learning and General-to-Specific Ordering of Hypotheses
title: Hypothesis Representation
content:
A hypothesis $h$ is written as a conjunction (AND) of constraints on each attribute, $h = \langle c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n \rangle$, where each constraint $c_i$ is one of:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em]
\item a \textbf{specific value} (e.g. Sunny) --- the attribute must equal exactly this value
\item \textbf{"?"} --- any value of this attribute is acceptable
\item \textbf{"$\varnothing$"} --- no value of this attribute is acceptable (this hypothesis rejects every instance)
\end{itemize}
An instance $x$ \textbf{satisfies} $h$ if, for every attribute, $x$'s value matches $h$'s constraint or the constraint is "?".

This is the same idea as a compound logical condition with AND, where each attribute either must match exactly, is left unrestricted, or makes the whole condition impossible to satisfy.

section: Concept Learning and General-to-Specific Ordering of Hypotheses
title: More-General-Than-Or-Equal-To Relation
content:
For two hypotheses $h_j$ and $h_k$ defined over the same attributes, $h_j$ is more-general-than-or-equal-to $h_k$, written $h_j \ge_g h_k$, if every instance that satisfies $h_k$ also satisfies $h_j$. If in addition some instance satisfies $h_j$ but not $h_k$, then $h_j$ is \textbf{strictly} more general than $h_k$, written $h_j >_g h_k$.

This is the same idea as a subset relation: $h_j \ge_g h_k$ means the set of instances accepted by $h_k$ is a subset of the set of instances accepted by $h_j$.

section: Concept Learning and General-to-Specific Ordering of Hypotheses
title: Find-S
content: Find-S is a concept learning algorithm that searches the hypothesis space and outputs the \textbf{most specific} hypothesis that is consistent with all the \textbf{positive} training examples. It starts from the most specific hypothesis $\langle \varnothing,\ldots,\varnothing \rangle$ and generalizes it, one attribute at a time, only when a positive example is not yet satisfied. Negative examples are completely ignored.

section: Concept Learning and General-to-Specific Ordering of Hypotheses
title: Find-S Algorithm
content:
\textbf{Input:} a set of training examples, each labeled positive or negative

\textbf{Output:} the most specific hypothesis $h$ consistent with all positive examples

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Initialize $h$ to the most specific hypothesis in $H$: $h = \langle \varnothing,\varnothing,\ldots,\varnothing \rangle$.
\item For each training example $x$: if $x$ is negative, ignore it and move to the next example.
\item If $x$ is positive, check every attribute constraint in $h$ against $x$.
\item For each constraint not satisfied by $x$: if the constraint is $\varnothing$, replace it with $x$'s value for that attribute; if it is a specific value different from $x$'s value, replace it with "?".
\item Repeat steps 2 to 4 for every remaining training example.
\item Output the final hypothesis $h$.
\end{enumerate}

title: Example 1.16 --- Tracing Find-S on a Weather Dataset
content:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ccc}
\toprule
Sky & AirTemp & EnjoySport \\
\midrule
Sunny & Warm & Yes \\
Sunny & Warm & Yes \\
Rainy & Cold & No \\
Sunny & Cold & Yes \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Trace Find-S on this dataset and give the final hypothesis.

\textbf{Solution:}
\[
h_0 = \langle \varnothing, \varnothing \rangle \quad \text{(initial, most specific)}
\]
\textbf{Example 1 (Sunny, Warm, Yes) --- positive:} both constraints are $\varnothing$, so update each to match.
\[
h_1 = \langle \text{Sunny}, \text{Warm} \rangle
\]
\textbf{Example 2 (Sunny, Warm, Yes) --- positive:} already matches $h_1$, no change.
\[
h_2 = \langle \text{Sunny}, \text{Warm} \rangle
\]
\textbf{Example 3 (Rainy, Cold, No) --- negative:} Find-S ignores negative examples.
\[
h_3 = h_2 = \langle \text{Sunny}, \text{Warm} \rangle
\]
\textbf{Example 4 (Sunny, Cold, Yes) --- positive:} Sky matches (Sunny), but AirTemp does not (Warm $\ne$ Cold), so generalize AirTemp to "?".
\[
h_4 = \langle \text{Sunny}, \, ? \rangle
\]
\boxed{\text{Final hypothesis: } h = \langle \text{Sunny}, \, ? \rangle}

Trace Find-S on this dataset and give the final hypothesis.

\textbf{Solution:}
\[
h_0 = \langle \varnothing, \varnothing \rangle
\]
\textbf{Example 1 (Red, Big, Yes) --- positive:} update both constraints from $\varnothing$ to match.
\[
h_1 = \langle \text{Red}, \text{Big} \rangle
\]
\textbf{Example 2 (Red, Big, Yes) --- positive:} already matches, no change.
\[
h_2 = \langle \text{Red}, \text{Big} \rangle

\[
h_3 = h_2 = \langle \text{Red}, \text{Big} \rangle
\]
\textbf{Example 4 (Red, Small, Yes) --- positive:} Color matches (Red), but Size does not (Big $\ne$ Small), so generalize Size to "?".
\[
h_4 = \langle \text{Red}, \, ? \rangle
\]
\boxed{\text{Final hypothesis: } h = \langle \text{Red}, \, ? \rangle}

section: Concept Learning and General-to-Specific Ordering of Hypotheses
title: Example 1.18 --- Tracing Find-S to the Most General Hypothesis
content:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ccc}
\toprule
Shape & Color & Target \\
\midrule
Round & Red & Yes \\
Round & Green & Yes \\
Square & Red & Yes \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Trace Find-S on this dataset and give the final hypothesis.

\textbf{Solution:}
\[
h_0 = \langle \varnothing, \varnothing \rangle
\]
\textbf{Example 1 (Round, Red, Yes) --- positive:} update both constraints from $\varnothing$ to match.
\[
h_1 = \langle \text{Round}, \text{Red} \rangle
\]
\textbf{Example 2 (Round, Green, Yes) --- positive:} Shape matches (Round), but Color does not (Red $\ne$ Green), so generalize Color to "?".
\[
h_2 = \langle \text{Round}, \, ? \rangle
\]
\textbf{Example 3 (Square, Red, Yes) --- positive:} Shape does not match (Round $\ne$ Square), so generalize Shape to "?"; Color is already "?", so it stays.
\[
h_3 = \langle \, ?, \, ? \rangle
\]
\boxed{\text{Final hypothesis: } h = \langle \, ?, \, ? \rangle}
Since every positive example forced a generalization, Find-S was pushed all the way to the most general hypothesis --- meaning no attribute in this small dataset was restrictive enough to separate positive from negative examples. \checkmark

title: Limitations of Find-S: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Find-S ignores
content:
\textbf{Limitations of Find-S:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Find-S \textbf{ignores negative examples entirely}, so it cannot detect if the training data is inconsistent (e.g. two identical instances labeled differently)
\item Find-S outputs only \textbf{one} hypothesis (the most specific one consistent with the positives); it cannot tell us whether this was the \textit{only} consistent hypothesis or one of many
\item Find-S has no way to know if it has converged to the true target concept, since it never checks negative examples for consistency
\item These limitations are exactly what motivate the \textbf{Candidate Elimination Algorithm} (Section 1.3), which tracks \textit{all} hypotheses consistent with \textit{both} positive and negative examples at once
\end{enumerate}

\newpage

section: Version Spaces and the Candidate Elimination Algorithm
title: Version Space
content:
Given a hypothesis space $H$ and a set of training examples $D$, the version space $VS_{H,D}$ is the subset of all hypotheses in $H$ that are consistent with every training example in $D$ --- that is, every hypothesis that correctly classifies every positive example as positive and every negative example as negative.

Find-S (Section 1.2.3) returns only \textbf{one} member of this set (the most specific one); the version space is the \textbf{entire} set of hypotheses that fit the data equally well.

section: Version Spaces and the Candidate Elimination Algorithm
title: Specific and General Boundary Sets
content:
Rather than listing every hypothesis in the (possibly huge) version space one by one, it is represented compactly using two boundary sets:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em]
\item \textbf{Specific boundary $S$:} the set of most specific hypotheses in the version space.
\item \textbf{General boundary $G$:} the set of most general hypotheses in the version space.
\end{itemize}
Every hypothesis $h$ satisfying $S \le_g h \le_g G$ for some member of each boundary is guaranteed to be in the version space, without needing to be listed individually.

\subsection{The Candidate Elimination Algorithm}

section: Version Spaces and the Candidate Elimination Algorithm
title: Candidate Elimination Algorithm
content:
\textbf{Input:} a set of training examples, each labeled positive or negative

\textbf{Output:} the boundary sets $S$ and $G$ describing the final version space

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Initialize $S$ to the most specific hypothesis in $H$: $S = \{\langle \varnothing,\ldots,\varnothing \rangle\}$.
\item Initialize $G$ to the most general hypothesis in $H$: $G = \{\langle ?,\ldots,? \rangle\}$.
\item For each training example $d$:
\item[] \textbf{If $d$ is positive:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.5em,itemsep=3pt]
\item Remove from $G$ any hypothesis inconsistent with $d$ (any hypothesis that rejects $d$).
\item For each hypothesis $s$ in $S$ inconsistent with $d$: remove $s$, and replace it with all of its minimal generalizations that are consistent with $d$ and are more specific than some hypothesis in $G$.
\item Remove from $S$ any hypothesis that is more general than another hypothesis in $S$.
\end{enumerate}
\item[] \textbf{If $d$ is negative:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.5em,itemsep=3pt]
\item Remove from $S$ any hypothesis inconsistent with $d$ (any hypothesis that accepts $d$).
\item For each hypothesis $g$ in $G$ inconsistent with $d$: remove $g$, and replace it with all of its minimal specializations that are consistent with $d$ and are more general than some hypothesis in $S$.
\item Remove from $G$ any hypothesis that is more specific than another hypothesis in $G$.
\end{enumerate}
\item Repeat step 3 for every remaining training example.
\item Return the final $S$ and $G$.
\end{enumerate}

section: Version Spaces and the Candidate Elimination Algorithm
title: Reading the Boundary Sets: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] $S$
content:
\textbf{Reading the Boundary Sets:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item $S$ always generalizes on \textbf{positive} examples only; $G$ always specializes on \textbf{negative} examples only
\item If $S=G$ and both contain exactly one hypothesis, the target concept has been \textbf{uniquely} identified (Examples 1.19, 1.20)
\item If $S$ and $G$ have not converged, \textbf{every} hypothesis lying between them (more general than $S$, more specific than $G$) is still a valid candidate, as enumerated in Example 1.21
\item Unlike Find-S, Candidate Elimination uses \textbf{both} positive and negative examples, so it can detect an inconsistent training set: this happens if $S$ or $G$ ever becomes empty
\end{enumerate}
